items.context: Kagiso pays R18 for a taxi to school and R18 for a taxi back home each school day.
items.prompt: Calculate the total daily taxi cost (there and back).
Kagiso attends school 5 days a week. Calculate the total weekly taxi cost.

items.context: Kagiso's father gives him a weekly allowance of R220.
items.prompt: Calculate how much money remains after paying for the week's taxi fares.
Convert the weekly taxi cost of R180 to cents, and calculate what percentage of R500 (50 000 cents) this represents.

Kagiso spends R180 a week on taxi fares. Determine the total over a 4-week month, then determine what a 12-week school term costs, and determine how many weeks of his R220 allowance that term cost equals.
items.answer: A 4-week month costs 4 × R180 = R720. A 12-week term costs 12 × R180 = R2 160. At R220 a week that is 2 160 ÷ 220 ≈ 9,8 weeks of allowance — so nearly ten weeks of his money goes on getting to school over a twelve-week term.
items.explanation: Multiply the weekly cost by the number of weeks. Dividing a total by a weekly amount converts it into weeks, which is a far clearer way to feel the size of a cost than a rand figure on its own.

items.prompt: Kagiso wants to save R150 per month toward a bicycle costing R1 000. He also receives a once-off R100 gift in month 2 only, added to his savings. Calculate how many WHOLE months of saving are needed to reach R1 000.
items.explanation: By month 5: (150 × 5) + 100 = R850 (not yet enough). By month 6: (150 × 6) + 100 = R1 000, which is enough. So 6 whole months are needed.

items.prompt: Kagiso's taxi fare increases by R4 per trip (each way) starting next term. Calculate the new daily taxi cost, and calculate this as a percentage increase on the original R36 daily cost (1.1), rounded to one decimal place.
items.explanation: New fare per trip = R18 + R4 = R22. New daily cost = R22 × 2 = R44. Increase = R44 − R36 = R8. Percentage increase = (8 ÷ 36) × 100 ≈ 22.2%.

items.prompt: The weekly taxi cost is R180 and the allowance R220. Determine the taxi cost as a percentage of the allowance, then determine what percentage it becomes once the fare rises to R22 each way, and state what Kagiso must give up.
items.answer: Now: 180 ÷ 220 × 100 ≈ 81,8%. After the rise the fare is R22 each way, so R44 a day and 5 × R44 = R220 a week — exactly 100% of his allowance. He must give up everything else: the R40 a week he currently has left for food or airtime disappears entirely.
items.explanation: Divide the cost by the allowance and multiply by 100. Recompute the whole chain after the rise rather than adjusting the percentage. The reasoning mark is for naming what the change costs him in practice, not just in percentage points.

items.prompt: Money Kagiso's father gives him each week is an example of...
items.explanation: Money received by Kagiso from his father is income for him.

items.prompt: Kagiso saves R150 a month and receives a once-off R80 bonus in month 3. Determine his savings after 4 months, then determine the month in which he first has the R1 000 for the bicycle, and determine what he has left over.
items.answer: After 4 months: 4 × R150 + R80 = R680. He first passes R1 000 in month 7, when he has 7 × 150 + 80 = R1 130 — so he buys the bicycle with R130 left over. In month 6 he has only R980, R20 short.
items.explanation: Add the monthly saving and include the once-off from the month it arrives. Check the month BEFORE as well as the month after: being R20 short in month 6 is what makes month 7 the answer, and the R130 is what he actually has in hand.

items.context: A rectangular bathroom floor measures 3.1 m long and 3 m wide.
items.prompt: Calculate the area of the bathroom floor.
Convert the floor's length of 3.1 m to centimetres, and calculate what percentage of a 500 cm maximum room length this represents.

items.context: The floor tiles measure 30 cm by 30 cm (0.3 m by 0.3 m).
items.prompt: The bathroom floor is 9,3 m² and each 30 cm by 30 cm tile covers 0,09 m². Determine how many tiles are needed to cover the floor, then state why the answer is not a whole number and what that means for buying.
items.answer: 9,3 ÷ 0,09 = 103,33 tiles. It is not a whole number because the floor is 3,1 m long and 30 cm does not divide into 3,1 m evenly — the last row has to be cut. For buying it means rounding UP to at least 104 tiles, and in practice more, because a cut tile wastes its offcut.
items.explanation: Divide the floor area by the area of one tile. A fractional answer signals that the tiles do not fit the room exactly, which is normal — it is why tiling always involves cutting, and why the purchase is always rounded up.

items.prompt: Tiles are sold in boxes of 10 tiles. Calculate the area covered by one box.

Tiles come in boxes covering 0,9 m² each and the floor is 9,3 m². Determine the minimum boxes and whether this exceeds the 9-box order limit, then determine how much floor one box more than the minimum would cover.
items.answer: Boxes = 9,3 ÷ 0,9 = 10,33 → 11 boxes, which does exceed the limit of 9 per order, so two orders are needed. Twelve boxes would cover 12 × 0,9 = 10,8 m² — 1,5 m² more than the floor needs, a sensible reserve for breakages and future repairs.
items.explanation: Divide the area by the coverage per box and round UP. The order limit is a separate constraint that changes how the tiles must be bought, not how many. Keeping a spare box is standard practice, since later batches rarely match in shade.

items.prompt: Each box costs R150. Calculate the cost of 11 boxes.
Eleven boxes cover 9,9 m² and the floor is 9,3 m². Determine the covered area as a percentage of the floor and the surplus, then state whether that waste is reasonable.
items.answer: Covered = 9,9 ÷ 9,3 × 100 ≈ 106,5% of the floor, so 9,9 − 9,3 = 0,6 m² is surplus. The waste is reasonable: it is under 7% of the floor, and some surplus is unavoidable, because tiles are sold in whole boxes and edge tiles must be cut.
items.explanation: Express what is bought against what is needed; the surplus is the difference. The judgement mark is for recognising that zero waste is impossible when a product comes in fixed quantities — the real question is whether the waste is small, and 7% is.

items.prompt: Which unit is most appropriate for measuring the bathroom floor's area?
items.explanation: A bathroom floor of a few square metres is best measured in m².

items.prompt: The tiles bought cover 9.9 m² and the floor needs 9.3 m². Calculate the wasted (excess) tiled area beyond what the floor needs, and state whether this exceeds 1 m².
items.answer: 0.6 m² — no, this does not exceed 1 m².
items.explanation: Wasted area = 9.9 m² − 9.3 m² = 0.6 m². Since 0.6 m² < 1 m², this does not exceed 1 m².

items.context: A classroom is drawn on a site plan at a scale of 1 : 80. On the plan, the classroom measures 9 cm by 7 cm.
items.prompt: Calculate the actual length and width of the classroom, in metres.
The classroom measures 9 cm by 7 cm on a 1 : 80 plan. Determine its actual floor area, then determine how many learners it holds at 1,2 m² each, and state whether a class of 40 fits.
items.answer: Actual: 9 × 80 = 720 cm = 7,2 m and 7 × 80 = 560 cm = 5,6 m, so the area is 7,2 × 5,6 = 40,32 m². At 1,2 m² each: 40,32 ÷ 1,2 = 33,6 → 33 learners. A class of 40 does NOT fit — the room is 7 learners short, needing a further 7 × 1,2 = 8,4 m² of floor.
items.explanation: Apply the scale to each length, then multiply for area. Capacity is area divided by the space one learner needs, rounded DOWN. Stating the shortfall in both learners and square metres is what makes the answer useful to a school.

items.prompt: A scale of 1 : 80 means...

options.label: 1 cm on the plan = 80 cm in real life
1 cm on the plan = 80 m in real life
80 cm on the plan = 1 cm in real life
The plan is 80 times bigger than real life

items.answer: 1 cm on the plan = 80 cm in real life
items.explanation: A scale of 1 : 80 means every 1 unit on the plan represents 80 of the same unit in real life.

items.context: The classroom's entrance faces East.
items.prompt: In which direction is directly opposite the entrance?
items.explanation: The direction directly opposite (180° from) East is West.

items.context: A stationery cupboard within the classroom measures 1.5 cm by 1 cm on the same plan.
items.prompt: Calculate the actual dimensions of the cupboard, in metres, and calculate the perimeter of the cupboard.
items.answer: Length = 1.2 m, Width = 0.8 m; Perimeter = 4 m.

items.prompt: A cupboard covers 0,96 m² in the 40,32 m² classroom. Determine what percentage of the floor it takes and whether this exceeds 5%, then determine how many such cupboards the 5% limit allows in total.
items.answer: Cupboard = 0,96 ÷ 40,32 × 100 ≈ 2,4% of the floor, which does not exceed 5%. Five percent of 40,32 m² is 2,016 m², and 2,016 ÷ 0,96 = 2,1, so at most 2 cupboards fit within the limit — one more than the room has now.
items.explanation: Express the cupboard against the floor area. To find how many fit inside a limit, convert the limit into square metres first, then divide by the area of one cupboard and round DOWN.

items.prompt: Write down the number of books borrowed in Week 4.
items.explanation: Read the value directly from the table.

items.prompt: Calculate the mean number of books borrowed per week over the 6 weeks.

Weekly borrowing was 15, 22, 12, 28, 33 and 38 books, with a mean of about 24,67. Determine the range and express it as a percentage of the mean, then state whether the librarian should plan for 25 books a week.
items.answer: Range = 38 − 12 = 26 books, which is 26 ÷ 24,67 × 100 ≈ 105,4% of the mean. The librarian should not plan for 25: borrowing has grown steadily to 38, so planning on the mean would leave the shelves short by 13 books in a week like Week 6.
items.explanation: Range is maximum minus minimum, expressed against the mean to show spread relative to size. A range larger than the mean is a strong signal of change, and on a rising series the latest week is the better planning figure.

items.prompt: Borrowing rose from 15 books in Week 1 to 38 in Week 6. Determine the percentage increase and state whether it more than doubled, then determine what Week 7 would be if the same average weekly growth continued.
items.answer: Increase = (38 − 15) ÷ 15 × 100 ≈ 153,3%, so borrowing has more than doubled. Average weekly growth = (38 − 15) ÷ 5 = 4,6 books, so Week 7 would be about 38 + 4,6 ≈ 43 books.
items.explanation: Percentage increase is (new − old) ÷ old × 100, on the ORIGINAL value. For a projection, divide the total rise by the number of GAPS — five between six weeks, not six — and add that to the latest value.

items.prompt: In which week were the fewest books borrowed?
items.explanation: Week 3 had the fewest books borrowed at 12, the smallest value in the table.

items.context: Of the 38 books borrowed in Week 6: 25 were fiction and 13 were non-fiction.
items.prompt: Of the 38 books borrowed in Week 6, 25 were fiction and 13 non-fiction. Determine the percentage that were fiction, then determine how many more non-fiction borrowings would make the two equal, and state what the librarian should order.
items.answer: Fiction: 25 ÷ 38 × 100 ≈ 65,8%. Non-fiction would need 12 more borrowings to reach 25 and match. The librarian should order more fiction: it is what learners actually borrow — nearly two books in three — and stocking to an even split would leave the popular shelves empty.
items.explanation: A percentage of the week is the part divided by 38, times 100. The difference between the two counts is what equality would require. The recommendation mark is for ordering to demand rather than to a balance that only looks tidy.

items.prompt: If one book from Week 6 is chosen at random, calculate the probability, as a percentage, that it is a non-fiction book.
If one of the 6 weeks is chosen at random, calculate the probability, as a percentage, that more than 25 books were borrowed that week.
items.explanation: Weeks with more than 25: Week 4 (28), Week 5 (33), Week 6 (38) — 3 weeks. (3 ÷ 6) × 100 = 50%.

items.prompt: Which type of graph would best display how borrowing changed week by week?

options.label: A single bar with no categories

items.explanation: A line graph best shows how a value changes over a sequence of time periods, such as weekly borrowing.

sections.title: The Khumalo Family's Data and Airtime Budget

items.context: The Khumalo family spends R350 on a monthly data bundle and R120 on airtime.
items.prompt: Calculate the total monthly spend on data and airtime.

items.context: The family's monthly income is R8 500.
items.prompt: Calculate the income remaining after the R470 spent on data and airtime.
Data costs R70 per GB. Calculate how many GB the R350 data budget buys.
Convert the 5 GB data bundle to MB (1 GB = 1 024 MB).
The family uses all 5 GB over 4 weeks. Determine the average GB used per week, then determine the average MB used per day over a 28-day month, and state whether a 1 GB weekly cap would be enough.
items.answer: Average = 5 ÷ 4 = 1,25 GB a week. Over 28 days: 5 120 MB ÷ 28 ≈ 182,9 MB a day. A 1 GB weekly cap would NOT be enough — they use 1,25 GB a week, so they would run out roughly a day and a half early every week.
items.explanation: Divide the bundle by the number of weeks for a weekly average, and convert to MB with 1 GB = 1 024 MB before dividing by days. The judgement mark is for comparing the cap against actual use and saying by how much it falls short, not merely that it does.

items.prompt: The family wants to save R500 per month toward a new phone costing R4 000. They also receive a R300 once-off gift in month 3, added to their savings. Calculate how many WHOLE months of saving are needed to reach R4 000.
items.explanation: By month 6: (500 × 6) + 300 = R3 300 (not yet enough). By month 7: (500 × 7) + 300 = R3 800 (still not enough). By month 8: (500 × 8) + 300 = R4 300, which is enough. So 8 whole months are needed.

items.prompt: The family upgrades to a bigger data bundle costing R70 more per month. Calculate the new total monthly spend on data and airtime, and calculate this as a percentage increase on the original total spend of R470 (1.1), rounded to one decimal place.
items.explanation: New data cost = R350 + R70 = R420. New total = R420 + R120 = R540. Increase = R540 − R470 = R70. Percentage increase = (70 ÷ 470) × 100 ≈ 14.9%.

items.prompt: The family spends R470 a month on data and airtime out of an income of R8 500. Determine this as a percentage of income, then determine what it becomes after the R70 upgrade, and state whether communication spending is a concern if 8% of income is the household limit.
items.answer: Original: 470 ÷ 8 500 × 100 ≈ 5,5%. After the upgrade: 540 ÷ 8 500 × 100 ≈ 6,4%. It is not yet a concern — both sit below the 8% limit — but the upgrade consumed about a third of the remaining room, moving the household from 2,5 percentage points under the limit to 1,6.
items.explanation: Divide the spend by income and multiply by 100 for each case. The judgement mark is for measuring how much room is left against the limit, rather than only checking that the limit is met — that is what shows whether the next upgrade is affordable.

items.prompt: Money spent on data and airtime is an example of...
items.explanation: Money paid out for data and airtime is an expense for the family.

items.prompt: The family saves R500 a month starting this month and receives a once-off R200 bonus in month 2. Determine their savings after 3 months, then determine the month in which the fund first reaches R3 700, and state how much later that would be without the bonus.
items.answer: After 3 months: 3 × R500 + R200 = R1 700. The fund reaches R3 700 in month 7, since 7 × 500 + 200 = R3 700. Without the bonus, 3 700 ÷ 500 = 7,4, so month 8 would be needed. The R200 brings the target forward by a whole month.
items.explanation: Add the regular saving month by month and drop the once-off amount in at the month it arrives. Round UP for whole months, since a part month does not complete the saving. The comparison shows the real value of a small once-off amount: not the R200 itself, but the month of waiting it removes.

items.context: A rectangular kitchen floor measures 4.5 m long and 3.2 m wide.
items.prompt: Calculate the area of the kitchen floor.
Convert the floor's length of 4.5 m to centimetres.

items.context: The floor tiles measure 40 cm by 40 cm (0.4 m by 0.4 m).
items.prompt: The kitchen floor is 14,4 m² and each 40 cm by 40 cm tile covers 0,16 m². Determine how many tiles cover the floor exactly, then state why the shop cannot sell that number.
items.answer: Tiles needed = 14,4 ÷ 0,16 = 90 exactly. The shop cannot sell 90, because tiles come in boxes of 8 and 90 ÷ 8 = 11,25 — the family must buy 12 boxes, which is 96 tiles, 6 more than the floor requires.
items.explanation: Divide the floor area by the area of one tile. The reasoning mark is for the packaging constraint: an exact answer in tiles becomes an inexact one in boxes, and the rounding up always happens at the box, never at the tile.

items.prompt: Tiles are sold in boxes of 8 tiles. Calculate the area covered by one box.

Tiles come in boxes of 8 covering 1,28 m² each, and the floor is 14,4 m². Determine the minimum number of boxes and how much extra floor they could tile, then state whether the supplier limit of 10 boxes per order is a problem.
items.answer: Boxes = 14,4 ÷ 1,28 = 11,25 → 12 boxes, covering 12 × 1,28 = 15,36 m², which is 0,96 m² more than the floor needs. The 10-box limit is a problem: 12 boxes cannot be bought on one order, so two orders are needed, with the risk that the second batch comes from a different production run and does not match in shade.
items.explanation: Divide the area by the coverage per box and round UP, since part of a box cannot be bought. The practical mark is for the supplier limit: an ordering rule can turn one purchase into two, and tiles in particular vary in colour between batches.

items.prompt: Each box costs R360. Calculate the cost of 12 boxes.

Twelve boxes cover 15,36 m² and the floor is 14,4 m². Determine the covered area as a percentage of the floor, then determine what percentage of the tiles bought is surplus, and explain why the two percentages differ.
items.answer: Covered as a percentage of the floor: 15,36 ÷ 14,4 × 100 ≈ 106,7%. Surplus as a percentage of what was bought: 0,96 ÷ 15,36 × 100 = 6,25%. They differ because they use different bases — 6,7% MORE than needed is the same 0,96 m² as 6,25% OF the purchase, since the purchase is the larger figure.
items.explanation: Always state what a percentage is a percentage OF. The same quantity measured against a smaller base gives a larger percentage; this is the single commonest source of confusion when comparing quantities bought against quantities needed.

items.prompt: Which unit is most appropriate for measuring the kitchen floor's area?
items.explanation: A kitchen floor of a few square metres is best measured in m².

items.prompt: The tiles supplied cover 15,36 m² and the floor needs 14,4 m². Determine the wasted area, then express that waste as a percentage of the floor, and say whether a tiler should treat this as a planning error or as a normal allowance.
items.answer: Waste = 15,36 − 14,4 = 0,96 m², which is 0,96 ÷ 14,4 × 100 ≈ 6,7% of the floor. That is a normal allowance rather than an error: tilers routinely order 5–10% extra for cuts at the edges and for breakages, and a job ordered with no spare at all stops the moment one tile cracks. Calling all 0,96 m² "waste" also misreads it — most of it leaves as offcuts that were never going to fit whole.
items.explanation: Subtract the area needed from the area supplied, then express the difference against the FLOOR rather than against the boxes, because the floor is what the customer is paying to cover. The judgement mark is for knowing what a normal cutting allowance looks like: the same 0,96 m² is careless on a 100 m² job and prudent on a 14 m² one.

items.context: A community hall is drawn on a site plan at a scale of 1 : 100. On the plan, the hall measures 8 cm by 6 cm.
items.prompt: Calculate the actual length and width of the hall, in metres.
The hall measures 8 cm by 6 cm on a 1 : 100 plan. Determine its actual floor area and how many people it seats at 1,2 m² each, then say whether a 6 m by 2 m stage is worth the seats it costs.
items.answer: 8 × 100 = 800 cm = 8 m and 6 × 100 = 600 cm = 6 m, so the area is 48 m², seating 48 ÷ 1,2 = 40 people. A 6 × 2 = 12 m² stage leaves 36 m², seating 30 — it costs 10 seats, a quarter of the hall. Whether that is worth it depends on the event: at a prizegiving, where everyone must see the front, a stage earns its space; at a meeting, where everyone must be seated, losing a quarter of the seats is a high price for a raised floor.
items.explanation: Apply the scale to each length, then divide USABLE area by the space one person needs — anything built into the room comes off before the division, not after. The judgement mark is for seeing that the same 12 m² is a good trade or a bad one depending on what the hall is being used for, which no calculation settles.

items.prompt: A scale of 1 : 100 means...

options.label: 1 cm on the plan = 100 cm in real life
1 cm on the plan = 100 m in real life
100 cm on the plan = 1 cm in real life
The plan is 100 times bigger than real life

items.answer: 1 cm on the plan = 100 cm in real life
items.explanation: A scale of 1 : 100 means every 1 unit on the plan represents 100 of the same unit in real life.

items.context: The hall's main entrance faces North.
items.prompt: In which direction is directly opposite the entrance?
items.explanation: The direction directly opposite (180° from) North is South.

items.context: A storage room within the hall measures 2 cm by 1.5 cm on the same plan.
items.prompt: The storage room measures 2 cm by 1,5 cm on the 1 : 100 plan. Determine its actual dimensions and perimeter, then determine how much skirting board is needed if a 0,8 m doorway needs none, and determine the cost at R45 per metre.
items.answer: Actual: 2 m by 1,5 m, so the perimeter is 2 × (2 + 1,5) = 7 m. Subtracting the 0,8 m doorway leaves 7 − 0,8 = 6,2 m of skirting, costing 6,2 × R45 = R279.
items.explanation: Apply the scale to each length, then use P = 2(l + b). Skirting follows the wall, not the doorway, so openings are subtracted from the perimeter before costing. Multiply the remaining length by the rate per metre.

items.prompt: Calculate the actual area of the storage room, and state whether this exceeds 10% of the hall's total floor area (48 m²).
items.answer: 3 m² — no, this does not exceed 10% of the hall (4.8 m²).
items.explanation: Storage room area = 2 m × 1.5 m = 3 m². 10% of 48 m² = 4.8 m². Since 3 m² < 4.8 m², this does not exceed 10% of the hall.

items.answer: Range = 48 − 18 = 30 packets, which is 30 ÷ 33 × 100 ≈ 90,9% of the mean. A range almost as large as the mean means sales are very uneven: ordering 33 packets every week would leave the shop short in the busiest weeks and holding unsold stock in the quietest, so orders should follow the recent trend rather than the average.
items.explanation: Range is maximum minus minimum; expressing it against the mean shows the spread relative to the size of the numbers. A range near 100% of the mean is a strong signal of variability — the same range would be trivial if the mean were 300 rather than 33.

items.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in packets sold from Week 1 to Week 6, and state whether sales have more than doubled over this period.
items.answer: 100% increase — no, sales have not MORE than doubled (they have exactly doubled).
items.explanation: Increase = 48 − 24 = 24. Percentage increase = (24 ÷ 24) × 100 = 100%. Since a 100% increase means the value doubled exactly, sales have not increased by MORE than double.

items.prompt: In which week were the fewest packets sold?
items.explanation: Week 3 had the fewest packets sold at 18, the smallest value in the table.

items.context: Of the 48 packets sold in Week 6: 20 were chips, 18 were biscuits, and 10 were sweets.
items.prompt: Calculate the percentage of Week 6 packets that were chips.
If one packet from Week 6 is chosen at random, calculate the probability, as a percentage, that it is a biscuit packet.

Of the 48 packets sold in Week 6, 20 were chips, 18 biscuits and 10 sweets. Determine the percentage that were sweets, then determine how many more sweet packets would have to sell to match biscuits, and state what the tuck shop should order given the whole six-week trend.
items.answer: Sweets: 10 ÷ 48 × 100 ≈ 20,8%. To match the 18 biscuit packets, 8 more sweet packets would have to sell. Given the trend, the shop should order more of everything rather than shifting between lines: weekly sales rose from 24 to 48 packets, a doubling, so the binding problem is total volume, not the split within a week.
items.explanation: A percentage of the week is the line divided by 48, times 100. The reasoning mark is for reading the within-week split against the between-week trend: a growing total matters far more for ordering than the proportions inside any single week.

questions.prompt: VAT in South Africa is charged at 15%. A bag of cement costs R95,00 before VAT. Calculate the VAT on one bag.
questions.explanation: VAT = 15% × R95,00 = 0,15 × 95 = R14,25. The VAT is only the tax part, not the new price.

questions.prompt: A kettle is marked R459,00 excluding VAT. Calculate its price including 15% VAT.
questions.explanation: Price including VAT = R459,00 × 1,15 = R527,85. Multiplying by 1,15 adds the 15% in one step; working out R68,85 and adding it gives the same answer.

questions.prompt: A till slip shows a total of R862,50, including 15% VAT. Calculate how much of the total is VAT.
questions.explanation: The total is 115% of the price before VAT, so the price before VAT = R862,50 ÷ 1,15 = R750,00. The VAT is R862,50 − R750,00 = R112,50. Taking 15% of R862,50 is the common mistake: it takes VAT on the VAT and gives R129,38.

questions.prompt: Thandi invests R12 000 at 8% per year compound interest for 3 years. Work out the value of the investment at the end of each year, and state what it is worth after 3 years.
questions.explanation: Each year's interest is worked out on the balance at the START of that year, and the closing balance is carried forward to become the next year's opening balance. That carrying forward is what makes it compound. A quick way to do each line is to multiply by 1,08, but the year-by-year working is what the method marks are for, and it is the only way to fill in the table a question like this usually asks for.

questions.prompt: Thandi invests R12 000 for 3 years at 8% per year. Calculate how much more the investment is worth under COMPOUND interest than under SIMPLE interest, and explain where the difference comes from.
questions.answer: Simple interest: 8% of R12 000 = R960,00 added each year, so after 3 years the value is R12 000 + 3 × R960,00 = R14 880,00. Compound interest, year by year: R12 960,00, then R13 996,80, then R15 116,54. The difference is R15 116,54 − R14 880,00 = R236,54. It comes from the interest EARNING interest: under simple interest every year's interest is worked out on the original R12 000, while under compound interest year 2 onwards is worked out on a balance that already includes the earlier interest.
questions.explanation: The two are identical after one year — R960,00 either way — and only separate from year 2, which is the point worth making in the explanation. The reasoning marks are for naming the mechanism rather than just reporting that compound is bigger.

questions.prompt: Nomsa is 41 years old and has a taxable income of R321 900,00 for the year. Calculate the annual tax payable after rebates, and hence the monthly PAYE deducted from Nomsa's salary.
questions.answer: From the table: R44 118 + 26% of (R321 900,00 − R245 100) = R64 086,00. At 41, Nomsa qualifies for the primary rebate only, totalling R17 820. Annual tax = R64 086,00 − R17 820 = R46 266,00. Monthly PAYE = R46 266,00 ÷ 12 = R3 855,50.
questions.explanation: The rebate is taken off the TAX, not off the income — subtracting it from R321 900,00 first would change which bracket applies and give a different, wrong answer. Dividing by 12 at the end turns the annual figure into what actually comes off a payslip each month.

questions.context: A Grade 10 class of 50 learners was asked how they travel to school. Walk: 14. Taxi: 22. Bus: 9. Car: 5.
questions.prompt: Calculate the angle of the sector that would represent taxi on a pie chart, correct to the nearest degree, and calculate the angle for bus. Then explain how you can check that all four angles have been worked out correctly.
questions.answer: Taxi: 22 ÷ 50 × 360 = 158°. Bus: 9 ÷ 50 × 360 = 65°. The check is that all four angles must add up to 360°, because the sectors together make one complete circle. (Rounding each to the nearest degree may make the total 359° or 361°, which is acceptable, but a total far from 360° means an error.)
questions.explanation: A pie chart divides 360° in the same ratio as the data divides the total, so every sector angle is "its share of the total, times 360". Work with the fraction before multiplying rather than converting to a percentage first — going via a rounded percentage loses accuracy twice. The check at the end is the one worth building a habit of: the angles of a pie chart must close the circle, and that catches an arithmetic slip in a single addition.

memo.text: the four angles must add to 360°, the whole circle

questions.context: A learner wants to find out how much time learners at her school spend on homework. She plans to ask: "You probably spend far too long on homework — how many hours do you waste on it each night?"
questions.prompt: Explain two separate problems with the wording of this question, and rewrite it so that it would collect useful data.
questions.answer: First, it is a leading question: "you probably spend far too long" tells the respondent what answer is expected, and people tend to agree with the suggestion put to them. Second, "waste" is loaded — it assumes homework has no value, which may push a respondent to overstate the time in order to agree, or understate it to disagree. A better wording: "How many hours did you spend on homework last night?"
questions.explanation: Data collection goes wrong before a single number is recorded, and the wording of the question is where it usually happens. A good question is neutral, uses no words that carry a judgement, and asks about something the respondent can actually recall — "last night" is answerable, while "usually" invites a guess. Two distinct faults must be named here, and "it is a bad question" counts as neither.

memo.text: it is a leading question: it suggests the answer
"waste" is a loaded word that assumes homework has no value
the rewording asks for a specific, recallable period such as "last night"

questions.context:
|+ Pass rate at a school, shown in a bar graph whose vertical axis runs from 60% to 68%
| Year | Pass rate |
|---|---|
| 2024 | 62% |
| 2025 | 66% |
questions.prompt: The principal says the bar graph shows the pass rate "shot up" last year, because the 2025 bar is three times the height of the 2024 bar. Calculate the actual percentage increase in the pass rate, explain why the bars give a misleading impression, and state what should be changed about the graph.
questions.answer: The actual rise is 66 − 62 = 4 percentage points, which as a percentage increase is 4 ÷ 62 × 100 = 6,45%. The bars mislead because the vertical axis starts at 60% rather than 0: only the part above 60 is drawn, so the visible heights are 2 units and 6 units, a ratio of 3 to 1, while the real figures are in the ratio 66 to 62. The axis should start at zero, so that the height of each bar is proportional to the value it represents.
questions.explanation: A truncated axis is the commonest way an honest set of numbers is made to tell a dishonest story, and it is worth being able to name. The test is simple: a bar graph claims that height is proportional to value, and that claim only holds if the axis starts at zero. Here it does not, so the eye compares 2 against 6 instead of 62 against 66. Note that the numbers themselves are not wrong — nothing has been faked. It is the drawing that misleads, which is why the fix is to the axis and not to the data.

memo.text: the vertical axis starts at 60%, not 0
so bar height is not proportional to the value: 2 units against 6 units
the axis should start at zero

| 20 ≤ m < 40 | 8 |

| 60 ≤ m < 80 | 11 |
| 80 ≤ m < 100 | 4 |
questions.prompt: State how many learners wrote the test, write down the modal class, and explain why this data must be drawn as a histogram with bars touching rather than as a bar graph with gaps between the bars.
questions.answer: 40 learners wrote the test, found by adding the frequencies: 3 + 8 + 14 + 11 + 4 = 40. The modal class is 40 ≤ m < 60, the interval with the highest frequency (14). The bars must touch because the marks are CONTINUOUS data: a mark of 40 sits exactly where one interval ends and the next begins, so there is no gap in the data and there must be no gap on the graph. A bar graph with gaps is for categories such as walk, taxi and bus, between which nothing exists.
questions.explanation: Continuous against categorical is the distinction that decides the whole shape of the drawing, and it is examined directly. Marks, heights, masses and times run without breaks, so their bars touch; modes of travel, favourite colours and provinces do not, so their bars are separated. Note that the modal CLASS is an interval, not a number — grouped data has thrown away the individual marks, so naming a single modal mark claims to know something the table no longer records.

memo.text: so there is no gap between intervals and the bars must touch

questions.prompt: Both towns are drawn on the same axes. Compare the two towns: calculate the difference between the highest and lowest temperature for each, identify the month where the two lines cross, and explain which town a visitor who dislikes temperature changes should choose, giving a reason based on the figures.
questions.answer: Town A: range = 26 − 16 = 10 °C. Town B: range = 26 − 23 = 3 °C. The two towns are the same in March, where both are 26 °C — this is where the two lines cross. The visitor should choose Town B: its range of 3 °C is far smaller than Town A's 10 °C, so its temperature stays much more even across the six months, which shows as a nearly flat line against Town A's rise and fall.
questions.explanation: Comparing two graphs means comparing their SHAPES, not just reading points off them. Two features carry the comparison here: where the lines cross, which is where the two quantities are equal, and how steeply each line moves, which the range measures numerically. Town A and Town B reach the same highest temperature, so a learner who compares only the peaks would conclude the towns are alike — the range is what shows they are not. questions.context: A shop wants to know how its customers travel to the shop. A researcher stands in the shop car park on a Saturday morning and asks 100 people how they travelled. 94 say they came by car.
questions.prompt: The shop concludes that 94% of its customers travel by car and decides to spend its budget on more parking. Explain why this sample is not representative, state what the conclusion would need to be valid, and suggest one better place to collect the data.
questions.answer: The sample is not representative because it was taken in the CAR PARK, so almost everyone in it arrived by car by definition — people who walked, took a taxi or came by bus would not pass through it. The conclusion would only be valid if every customer had an equal chance of being asked. Asking at the shop entrance or at the till, where all customers pass regardless of how they arrived, would give a better sample.
questions.explanation: The number 94% is perfectly accurate for the people who were asked; the problem is who was asked. A sample is biased when the way it is collected makes some group more likely to appear than it should, and standing in a car park does exactly that — it selects for car drivers before a single question is asked. Note also the Saturday morning: shoppers on a weekday after work may travel quite differently. The fix is always the same in principle, which is to sample where the whole population passes.

memo.text: the sample was taken in the car park, so it selects car users
people who walked, took a taxi or came by bus could not be included
every customer would need an equal chance of being asked
ask at the entrance or the till, where all customers pass

questions.context: The nine staff at a small business earn, in thousands of rand per month: 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 130.
questions.prompt: The owner advertises that "the average salary here is over R20 000 a month". Calculate the mean and the median of the nine salaries, and explain why quoting the mean here is misleading about what a new employee could expect to earn.
questions.answer: Mean = 180 ÷ 9 = 20 thousand, that is about R20 000 a month. Median = the fifth value when they are in order = 6 thousand, that is R6 000 a month. The median is far more honest here. One salary of R130 000 — the owner's own — is an outlier that drags the mean up above every other salary in the business: eight of the nine staff earn less than the mean. A new employee would join the group earning around R6 000, which is what the median describes.
questions.explanation: The owner's claim is not a lie; the mean really is over R20 000. That is what makes this worth practising — a statistic can be arithmetically correct and still mislead, and the skill is saying exactly how. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value pulls it a long way; the median only cares about position, so one enormous salary moves it by one place at most. When a distribution has an outlier, the median is the fairer summary, and "eight of the nine earn less than the mean" is the sentence that proves it.

memo.text: the R130 000 salary is an outlier that pulls the mean up
the median is more honest: eight of the nine staff earn less than the mean

questions.context: Two cellphone packages are drawn as two straight lines on one set of axes, showing cost against minutes used. Package A costs R150 per month plus R0,9 per minute. Package B has no monthly fee and costs R1,4 per minute.
questions.prompt: Compare the two packages. Calculate the cost of each for 200 minutes, determine the number of minutes at which the two graph lines cross, and advise a user who talks for about 500 minutes a month which package to choose, with a reason.
questions.answer: At 200 minutes: A = R150 + 200 × R0,9 = R330; B = 200 × R1,4 = R280. The graphs cross where the costs are equal: 150 + 0,9m = 1,4m, so 150 = 0,5m and m = 300 minutes. For 500 minutes, Package A costs R600 and Package B costs R700, so Package A is cheaper by R100. A user talking about 500 minutes is well past the crossing point at 300 minutes, where A becomes the cheaper of the two.
questions.explanation: The point where two cost graphs cross is the break-even point, and it is the single most useful thing to read off a pair of tariff graphs: below it one package wins, above it the other does. Package B is cheaper at first because it has no monthly fee, but its steeper line — R1,40 a minute against R0,90 — means it overtakes. Notice that the advice must name which side of the break-even point the user falls on; saying "A is cheaper" without that is a statement about one number rather than a reason.

memo.text: 500 minutes is past the crossing point at 300 minutes, where A becomes cheaper

questions.prompt: Calculate Thandi's total travelling time including the wait, and determine the latest time she can leave home to arrive at the clinic by 09:30. She wants to arrive 10 minutes early, so work to an arrival time of 09:20.
questions.answer: Travelling time = 8 + 26 + 12 = 46 minutes, plus 15 minutes waiting = 61 minutes, which is 1 hour 1 minutes. Working back from 09:20: 09:20 − 1 hour = 08:20, then − 1 minutes = 08:79. So she must leave home by 07:59.
questions.explanation: Route planning is addition and subtraction of times, and the two places marks are lost are both about minutes rather than method. First, the waiting time is part of the journey — a stage where nothing moves still takes time, and leaving it out makes her late. Second, subtract the hour and the minutes separately and borrow properly: 09:20 minus 21 minutes is not 09:01 but 08:59, because there are 60 minutes in an hour and not 100. Working back from the arrival time, rather than forward from a guess, is what makes the answer a single definite time.

memo.text: 61 minutes in total, or 1 hour 1 minutes

questions.prompt: A square vegetable patch has sides of 6,4 m. Calculate the perimeter of the patch.
questions.explanation: All four sides of a square are equal, so the perimeter is simply four times one side. There is no need for the rectangle formula, although 2(6,4 + 6,4) gives the same answer.

questions.prompt: A triangular flower bed has sides measuring 4,2 m, 5,6 m, 6,3 m. Calculate the perimeter of the flower bed.
questions.explanation: A triangle has no perimeter formula to remember — you simply add the three sides. That is true of any shape whose sides are all given: perimeter is always the sum of the outside edges, and the formulae for rectangles and circles are just shortcuts for shapes where the sides repeat.

questions.prompt: An L-shaped room is formed by taking a rectangle 8 m by 6 m and removing a 3 m by 2 m rectangle from one corner. Calculate the perimeter of the L-shaped room.
questions.context: Walking around the outside of the room from the bottom-left corner, the six walls are: 8 m along the bottom, then 4 m up the right-hand side, then 3 m to the left into the corner that was removed, then 2 m up, then 5 m to the left along the top, then 6 m down the left-hand side back to the start.
questions.explanation: An L-shape has no formula, so the only method is to walk the outline and add every wall. The two walls that are not given directly are found by subtraction: the right-hand side is 6 − 2 and the top is 8 − 3, because the piece that was cut away accounts for the difference. Working out those missing sides is where the method marks are.

questions.prompt: A builder claims that an L-shaped room made by cutting a 3 m by 2 m corner out of a 8 m by 6 m rectangle has a smaller perimeter than the full rectangle, and so needs less skirting board, because it is a smaller room. Show by calculation whether the builder is right, and explain the result.
questions.answer: Full rectangle: P = 2(8 + 6) = 28 m. L-shaped room, walking the outline: 8 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 5 + 6 = 28 m. The two perimeters are equal, so the builder is wrong — the L-shaped room needs exactly the same length of skirting. The room IS smaller: it covers 42 m² instead of 48 m². Cutting the corner out replaces two pieces of wall with two new pieces of exactly the same total length — the 3 m and the 2 m that now face into the notch are the same lengths that were removed from the top wall and the right-hand wall.
questions.explanation: This is worth more than the arithmetic. Cutting a rectangular notch out of a corner moves wall inward without lengthening or shortening it: every centimetre taken off the top wall reappears as wall running into the notch, and the same for the side. So a rectilinear shape cut from a corner always has the perimeter of the rectangle it started in, however much floor it loses. A builder quoting skirting by floor size would under-order every time.

Floor covered does fall, from 48 m² to 42 m²

questions.prompt: A window is made of a rectangle 1,2 m wide and 1,5 m high with a semicircle on top, the flat edge of the semicircle being the top of the rectangle. Calculate the perimeter of the window. Use π = 3,14.
questions.answer: The outside is made of the bottom of the rectangle, its two sides and the curved half of the circle. Curved part = ½ × πd = ½ × 3,14 × 1,2 = 1,884 m. P = 1,2 + 2(1,5) + 1,884 = 6,084 m
questions.explanation: The trap here is the top of the rectangle. It is a line on the drawing, but it is not on the OUTSIDE of the window, so it is not part of the perimeter — including it adds 1,2 m of glazing strip that does not exist. Half a circumference uses the diameter, not the radius: ½ × πd. And only the curved edge of the semicircle is halved; the three straight sides are used in full.

memo.text: Three straight sides added, the top of the rectangle excluded

questions.prompt: Sipho is 1,80 m tall and his BMI is 31,2. He plans to bring his BMI down to 25 in 4 weeks. Calculate how much mass he would need to lose, and evaluate whether his plan is sensible.
questions.answer: His mass now = 31,2 × 1,80² = 31,2 × 3,24 = 101,1 kg. At a BMI of 25 his mass would be 25 × 3,24 = 81,0 kg. He must lose 101,1 − 81,0 = 20,1 kg. In 4 weeks that is about 5,0 kg a week -- far above the safe rate of at most 1 kg a week. At a safe rate the loss would take at least 21 weeks, about 5 months. The goal is reasonable; the time frame is not.
questions.explanation: Two masses are needed: the one he has now, from his current BMI, and the one that gives a BMI of 25. Their difference is the loss. Evaluating the plan then means comparing the weekly rate it demands with the safe rate given -- a judgement the numbers support, not an opinion.

questions.prompt: The box-and-whisker diagram shows how long commuters waited for a taxi at a rank one morning. Write down the median waiting time, and calculate the interquartile range.
questions.answer: Median = 8 minutes, the line inside the box. Interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartile = 13 − 5 = 8 minutes.
questions.explanation: The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, so the interquartile range is simply the length of the box. It is the spread of the middle half of the waiting times, and unlike the range it is not pulled about by one unusually long wait.

questions.prompt: A savings account offers 6.5% simple interest per year. If Nomvula invests R8 000, how much interest will she earn after 3 years?
questions.context: First find one year's interest, then multiply by the number of years — with simple interest, every year earns interest on the original R8 000 only, never on interest already earned.
questions.explanation: One year's interest: R8 000 × 6.5 ÷ 100 = R520. Over 3 years: R520 × 3 = R1 560. Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount each year, unlike compound interest.
